readerTitle: Your sales just jumped 60%. Do you hire 50 people?
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (주방용품 도매·소매 회사 한 곳의 1년) · 모든 인물과 수치는 설명용
insight: 성장기의 채용은 '몇 명'을 정하는 문제가 아니라, 어떤 신호가 보일 때 누구를 먼저 뽑고, 그 사람들이 어떻게 빠르게 일하게 할지를 차례로 정하는 문제다.
misconception: 매출이 늘면 그만큼 사람을 한꺼번에 뽑아야 하고, 사람만 충분하면 성장 문제는 해결된다.

sources.text: 이 단원(ENT-06)의 개념 레슨: 조기 확장, 성장 앞선 채용, 창업자에서 CEO로, 프로세스 추가, 규모에서의 소통
모든 인물, 회사, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 가상입니다. 직원 28명, 매출 60% 증가, 오배송 100건 중 1건→4건, 연말 채용 34명(28+34=62명)이 카드 사이에서 서로 맞는지 확인했습니다. 실제 통계로 읽히지 않도록 카드에 illustrative 표시를 했습니다.
다음 레슨 예고 문구는 다음 단원 첫 레슨 제목이 확정되면 맞춰 바꾸세요.

cards.title: Your sales just jumped 60%. Do you hire 50 people?
body: Mara runs a kitchenware business: one warehouse, two shops of her own, and 120 independent stores that reorder from her. She has 28 staff.
Last year a regional chain started stocking her range. Sales rose 60%. Orders are shipping late. Her lender says, "Hire 50 people this year, or you'll lose it."
You're Mara for the next four decisions.

image.label: A crowded warehouse with boxes piling up and a small team
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 창고에 주방용품 상자가 천장까지 쌓여 있고, 직원 몇 명이 바쁘게 움직임. 한쪽 벽에 "Late orders" 메모가 붙은 화이트보드. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: The 50-person plan
body: The chain's orders are big, but it signed for one season only. Your other stores are reordering a bit more than last year. How do you plan hiring?

options.text: Hire all 50 by spring so you're ready for anything
options.feedback: You'd clear the backlog fast. But payroll nearly triples before the chain renews, and if it doesn't, you're cutting people by autumn.

options.text: Hire in waves, each one unlocked by a signal you set now: renewed contracts, backlog over a week, repeat orders
options.feedback: You grow staff as demand proves itself. You give up some speed, and the signals must be decided before emotions run high.

options.text: Hire no one and pay overtime until things settle
options.feedback: Cash stays safe. But tired people make mistakes, late orders keep coming, and the stores that loyally reorder start looking elsewhere.

cards.title: Who goes first?
body: Say you chose waves. The backlog signal is already met, so wave one is 12 people.
Right now every purchase order, schedule change and customer complaint still goes through you. Who are the first 12?

options.text: 12 pickers and drivers to ship the backlog
options.feedback: Boxes move faster this month. But 40 people now wait on your approval for everything, and you become the bottleneck.

options.text: An operations manager and two shift leads first, then pickers
options.feedback: Shipping improves a few weeks later, but decisions stop queuing at your desk. Your job shifts from doing the work to building the team that does it.

options.text: A head of marketing to keep growth coming
options.feedback: More demand poured into a jammed warehouse means more late orders and angrier customers.

cards.title: Mistakes are creeping in.
body: Say you hired the operations manager. Output is up. But wrong shipments rose from 1 in 100 orders to 4 in 100. Most errors happen at two steps: picking similar items and labeling boxes.

options.text: A manager signs off on every order before it ships
options.feedback: Errors drop, and so does speed. You've rebuilt the old bottleneck with a new name on it.

options.text: A barcode scan at picking and a short checklist at labeling, nothing else
options.feedback: Process goes only where mistakes repeat. Everyone else keeps working the way they did.

options.text: Remind everyone at the morning meeting to be careful
options.feedback: Free and friendly. But with a third of the staff brand new, good intentions don't replace a system.

cards.title: The new people don't know why.
body: Say you added scans and checklists. Errors fall back to about 1 in 100. By summer you're at 45 people.
Now you notice new staff chase whatever looks urgent. Two teams just promised the same truck to different customers.

options.text: Route all scheduling decisions back to you for consistency
options.feedback: No more clashes, but everything slows to the speed of one person, and your managers stop deciding.

options.text: A weekly note with three priorities and the reasons, plus one shared truck schedule each team owns
options.feedback: People decide on their own and still pull the same way. It costs you an hour a week of writing, every week.

options.text: Trust managers to pass the message down
options.feedback: Faster than doing it yourself, but each retelling drifts a little. By the third layer, the priorities differ.

cards.title: Not 50 people. 34.
body: The chain renewed, so wave two went ahead. A slow autumn kept wave three on hold. Mara ended the year with 62 people, not 78.
Orders ship on time again. She spends her days on suppliers and the next big customer, not on truck schedules.

image.label: Staircase chart: staff added in steps as signals appear
image.brief: 계단형 그래프. 가로축은 월, 세로축은 직원 수. 신호가 생길 때마다 한 칸씩 오름. 계단 옆 라벨: "Backlog signal", "Contract renewed", "Wave 3 on hold". 점선으로 '50명 한꺼번에' 직선 경로를 비교로 표시.

cards.softwareNote: In a software company the waves might be unlocked by retention, not backlog: hire the second support team only when new customers keep paying for three months, not when signups spike.

cards.title: Waves have costs too.
body: Good hires can take months to find. If you wait for every signal, a competitor may serve the demand first.
Staged hiring works best when signals are clear and agreed in advance. If the demand is truly locked in, such as a signed multi-year contract, hiring ahead of it can be the right call.
The goal isn't to hire slowly. It's to hire **on evidence**, not on hope.

cards.title: Scale in steps, and change how you lead at each step.
body: Each decision matched one idea from this unit.
list: **Waves, not 50 at once:** avoid premature scaling; hire ahead of growth only when it's proven
**Managers before more hands:** from founder to CEO
**Scans where errors repeat:** add process only where it pays
**Weekly priorities with reasons:** communicate at scale and keep your speed
cards.callout: **Try it today:** write the three signals that would justify your next hire. Decide them before you need them.
